# Threat—of AI

# *A new AI documentary captures the technology’s promise and peril—and shows why Congress cannot afford to stay passive.*

##### Are you an apocaloptimist? After 104 minutes of “The AI Doc,” Focus Features’ latest film, you might become one.

##### The movie—properly known as “The AI Doc: Or How I Became an Apocaloptimist ”—covers the full sweep of the artificial intelligence (AI) debate without oversimplifying it. It portrays a future where AI cures cancer and gives every child access to a world-class education. It also forecasts a future where advanced models can shut down society entirely.

##### If you are a Congressional staffer, you need to see it. If you’re not a Congressional staffer, you still need to see it.

##### The film spotlights doomers like Eliezer Yudkowsky  (who believe AI poses an existential threat to humanity) and accelerationists like Sam Altman  (who argue the answer is to build faster, not slower) without resolving their tension. It questions whether we can keep the most powerful AI models in American hands.

### Authoritarian AI and Chinese Technology Theft

##### Authoritarian countries are barreling ahead, infusing AI into all aspects of their governments. That includes suppressing their own populations and antagonizing enemies abroad. AI-enabled facial recognition technology in Iran, Russia, and China is shifting authoritarian repression from reactive to predictive, allowing regimes to identify and disrupt dissent before it materializes. Meanwhile, as Center for Humane Technology President Tristan Harris  explains in the film, Iran and Russia are already producing disinformation at scale, eroding trust in Western democratic institutions rather than trying to persuade outright.

##### The authoritarian AI threat is real across the board—but the movie reveals how China operates at a different order of magnitude. Beijing is not just using AI to repress and deceive; it is running an industrial-scale campaign to steal the American AI technology that makes our lead possible in the first place. That theft has immediate consequences for national security.

##### Last month, the top AI companies, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, put their intense competition aside and banded together under the Frontier Model Forum  to confront a common threat: Chinese IP theft. By

![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

##### have repeatedly stolen capabilities from America’s most advanced models, acquiring cutting-edge AI on the cheap rather than investing in the research themselves.

### Frontier AI Risks and Cybersecurity Threats

##### The movie itself is prescient, identifying the urgency of the problems AI presents. Last month, Anthropic announced that its latest model, Mythos Preview , is too dangerous to release publicly. Mythos has already identified thousands of previously undetected software vulnerabilities across every major operating system and browser. If this technology falls into the wrong hands before defenses are in place, the consequences would be severe.

##### Anyone watching “The AI Doc” is likely to agree that Congress should give federal agencies the tools to identify, expose, and sanction the foreign entities stealing American AI—and ensure the companies building it have a government partner. It’s a national security imperative.

##### The film ends with a direct challenge to its audience: get involved, push your government, don’t leave AI governance to the experts alone. It’s a reasonable ask. But the government they’re being asked to push is not meeting the moment.

### US AI Governance and National Security Gaps

##### At the exact time when the federal government should be surging capacity to counter adversarial AI misuse, it is cutting it . The gutting of the National Institute of Standards and Technology  (NIST) and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) leaves the United States less able to detect, mitigate, and respond to an emerging class of AI-enabled cyber-attacks with next to no human involvement.

##### The Center for AI Standards and Innovation—the primary government interface between Washington and the AI industry—operates  with 10 percent of the staff of the United Kingdom’s  equivalent institution. We are not keeping pace with allies, let alone adversaries.

##### The Trump administration’s AI Action Plan  rightly recommended the creation of an AI information sharing and analysis center (AI-ISAC) to coordinate public-private threat intelligence, but there is no timeline for standing it up. In the meantime, the government remains dependent on private companies voluntarily disclosing the threats they face. Potentially worst of all, the Pentagon is still feuding with Anthropic, which it has labeled a supply chain risk and blacklisted , banning defense contractors from using one of America’s best AI models.

### Congress Must Strengthen AI Security Capacity

##### Congress can help. See this movie and recognize that CISA and NIST should be funded to meet their

![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

##### Additionally, reserving “supply chain risk” designations for foreign adversary companies like Huawei and Kaspersky—not the American lab that just handed the security community its most powerful tool. Petty feuds are a gift to adversaries.

##### For some, the sheer intensity of the AI debate—between those who see existential catastrophe and those who see limitless possibility—produces whiplash, and whiplash produces inaction. Congressional staffers and their bosses don’t have that option. The film has a name for what this moment demands: apocaloptimists. People who are clear-eyed enough to see the risks and bold enough to act anyway.
